strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of molecular generation: jointly producing 3D geometry and explicit synthesis-oriented representations. Combining building-block reaction graphs with atomic coordinates is a meaningful extension of existing multimodal generators.

SYNSPACE represents substantial data-curation effort, containing 622,766 molecular reaction graphs and approximately 3.36 million conformers. Explicit reaction-center labels address ambiguity when building blocks have multiple potential coupling sites.

The reported unconditional results are promising: 96.7% chemical validity, 87.2% PoseBusters validity, and 50%/72% retrosynthesis solve rates. Retraining SemlaFlow on SYNSPACE provides a useful partial control for dataset effects.
Zero-shot fragment linking demonstrates useful flexibility, and the sampling and training ablations provide evidence that chemical constraints and self-conditioning improve performance.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains substantial unresolved inconsistencies. The categorical probabilities in Equations 16–17 sum to 1/(1−αt), rather than one, and disagree with Equation 2. Appendix B.7 specifies αt=exp(−10^8 t), which would mask essentially everything at almost every sampled training time. Algorithm 5 omits the 1/t factor expected when converting an endpoint prediction into the velocity of the stated linear interpolation. These may be documentation errors, but they prevent reliable reconstruction of the actual method.

The evaluation does not isolate the benefit of joint reaction–coordinate modeling. Most baselines use different training distributions, and there is no matched synthesis-aware generator followed by conventional conformer generation, nor a separately trained sequential graph-to-coordinate baseline. FinalOnly changes inference for the joint model and does not resolve this comparison. The closest synthesis-and-geometry co-design work is discussed but not empirically compared.

Claims of ensured practical synthesizability exceed the evidence. Appendix A.1 explicitly omits protection requirements, directing effects, and stoichiometry, while simplifying boronic acids to boranes. Template compatibility and independent retrosynthesis success do not validate the particular proposed multistep routes. Route-level expert assessment or experimental evidence is absent, and evaluation is restricted to 93 building blocks, 19 templates, and short assembly sequences.

The broad state-of-the-art conformer-quality claim is not supported consistently. The xTB metric measures only dispersion energy, whose reduction across different molecules does not establish overall conformational accuracy or low strain. Table 4 shows weaker distributional fidelity than several baselines on multiple metrics. On fixed-graph conformer generation, Table 5 favors RDKit on both COV and MAT; moreover, Appendix B.12 defines coverage over generated conformers, measuring proximity to references rather than coverage of the reference ensemble.

Fragment-linking evidence is limited to three selected targets and shows substantial trade-offs. SYNCOGEN achieves only 46.9–57.6% chemical validity versus 93.7–95.8% for DiffLinker, with lower PoseBusters validity on two targets. Docking and selected AlphaFold3 overlays do not establish binding efficacy, and the evaluation lacks aggregate anchor-preservation and successful-linking measurements. Allowing the supposedly fixed fragments to move during the final sampling steps further warrants explicit geometric evaluation.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting need improvement. SemlaFlow training is variously described as matching SYNCOGEN's epochs, using 200 epochs, and using 150 epochs. Dataset splits and held-out generalization protocols are insufficiently specified. Although three sampling runs are mentioned, uncertainty is not reported, including for retrosynthesis estimates based on only 100 molecules. These issues, together with the sampling inconsistencies, leave the promising results insufficiently substantiated for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap: jointly generating molecular geometry and explicit reaction-based representations. Reaction-center labels and handling variable atom counts within masked building blocks are useful design contributions.
SYNSPACE represents substantial dataset construction effort, with 622,766 reaction graphs and approximately 3.36 million conformers, including semi-empirical geometry optimization.

The reported unconditional results are promising: 96.7% chemical validity, 87.2% PoseBusters validity, and higher retrosynthesis solve rates than the evaluated baselines. Retraining SemlaFlow on SYNSPACE and including training and sampling ablations are valuable controls.
Zero-shot fragment linking demonstrates useful flexibility beyond unconditional generation, although its current evaluation remains preliminary.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. The categorical probabilities in Equations 16–17 sum to 1/(1−αt), rather than one, and disagree with Equation 2. Appendix B.7 specifies αt=exp(−10^8 t), which effectively masks everything for almost all sampled training times. Algorithm 5 also omits the usual 1/t factor when converting a clean-coordinate prediction into the velocity for the stated linear interpolation. These may be documentation errors, but the implemented training and sampling processes cannot be reliably reconstructed from the manuscript.

The experiments do not establish the benefit of joint modeling over a simpler synthesis-aware graph generator followed by conformer generation. No such pipeline baseline is evaluated under the same building-block and reaction vocabulary. The FinalOnly ablation changes inference for an already jointly trained model and does not replace this comparison. Comparisons with existing synthesis-aware generators, and stronger positioning against the cited concurrent synthesis/3D co-design work, are also needed.

Most unconditional baselines operate on a different chemical distribution and a much less constrained output space. This confounds comparisons of synthesizability, geometry, and distributional fidelity. The same-dataset SemlaFlow control helps, but its training description is inconsistent: the main text claims matching epochs, whereas Appendix C reports 150 epochs and a single conformer per molecule, versus 100 epochs and random conformer selection for SYNCOGEN. The assertion that the training procedure alone explains the gains is therefore unsupported.

Practical synthesizability is overstated. Appendix A.1 acknowledges omitted protection requirements, directing-group effects, and stoichiometry. Template compatibility and successful retrosynthetic searches do not validate the particular generated routes or establish reliable multi-step execution. No systematic expert route assessment, reaction-success validation, or experimental synthesis supports claims that the method ensures readily synthesizable products.

The evidence for superior conformer quality is mixed. Appendix D.2 reveals that the xTB metric measures only dispersion energy; lower dispersion energy across different molecules does not establish lower strain or greater physical plausibility. Table 4 shows worse distributional agreement than several baselines, including worse energy-distribution agreement than same-dataset SemlaFlow. Table 5 also favors RDKit on both reported metrics, and its COV definition measures generated-to-reference proximity rather than coverage of the reference ensemble.

The downstream evaluation uses only three selected complexes whose ligands match the small vocabulary. Table 6 reports only 46.9–57.6% chemical validity for SYNCOGEN, versus 93.7–95.8% for DiffLinker; PoseBusters results are mixed, and all three xTB values favor DiffLinker under the stated lower-is-better convention. Docking scores and selected AlphaFold3 overlays do not establish binding activity or accurate preservation of the conditioned geometry, particularly because the fixed coordinates are released during the final sampling steps.

Statistical support and generalization evidence are limited. Retrosynthesis rates use only 100 generated examples, without uncertainty estimates; although baseline sampling is averaged over three runs, variability is not reported. The evaluation remains restricted to 93 building blocks, 19 templates, and short synthesis trees, with no convincing scaling or held-out chemical-space study. Overall, the promising representation and dataset do not outweigh the unresolved methodological and evaluation issues at a top-tier conference threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap between synthesis-aware molecular generation and 3D geometric modeling. Jointly generating building-block identities, reaction-center labels, and coordinates is a useful contribution, particularly for geometry-conditioned design.
SYNSPACE represents substantial data-curation effort: 622,766 reaction graphs and approximately 3.36 million conformers, with explicit mappings between building blocks and product atoms.

The same-dataset SemlaFlow comparison provides encouraging evidence: SYNCOGEN improves chemical validity from 72.0% to 96.7%, PoseBusters validity from 60.3% to 87.2%, and Syntheseus solve rate from 48% to 72%. The ablations also demonstrate the practical importance of chemical constraints and self-conditioning.
Zero-shot fragment linking is a promising demonstration of the joint representation's flexibility, and the appendix provides substantial implementation and evaluation detail.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. The categorical distributions in Equations (16)–(17) are not normalized as written; the clean-state coefficient should involve alpha_s minus alpha_t. Appendix B.7 specifies alpha_t = exp(-10^8 t), which would mask essentially everything throughout almost the entire interval, contradicting the described progressive denoising. Algorithm 5 also omits the 1/t factor expected when converting clean-coordinate predictions into the velocity for the stated linear interpolation. These may be documentation errors, but they prevent faithful reproduction and leave the implemented generative process unclear.

The evaluation does not establish the benefit of joint modeling over a strong synthesis-aware pipeline. Most baselines generate unrestricted atomic graphs and are trained on different chemical distributions. Retraining SemlaFlow is valuable, but no reaction-based generator followed by ETKDG or a learned conformer generator is evaluated. The FinalOnly ablation does not replace this comparison. Consequently, improvements attributable to restricted chemistry, hard constraints, and joint learning remain insufficiently separated.

Claims of ensured synthesizability and readily executable routes exceed the evidence. Appendix A explicitly omits protection requirements, selectivity effects, and other practical reaction considerations. Retrosynthesis solve rates assess whether an external planner finds some route, rather than validating the generated route itself. Experimental synthesis is not essential, but independent expert assessment or route-level validation is needed to support the stronger claims.

The geometry metrics do not justify broad state-of-the-art claims. The reported xTB metric is only dispersion energy, whose reduction across different molecules does not establish better conformational accuracy or lower strain. Table 4 shows that SYNCOGEN is not consistently best on bond, angle, dihedral, or energy-distribution fidelity. Table 5 evaluates only 50 molecules and reports lower performance than ETKDG; moreover, its purported coverage formula measures generated-to-reference precision rather than reference-conformer coverage.

The downstream evaluation is limited to three selected complexes containing compatible vocabulary fragments. Fragment-linking validity is only 46.9–57.6%, versus 93.7–95.8% for DiffLinker, and PoseBusters performance is mixed. Docking scores and selected AlphaFold3 overlays provide preliminary evidence but do not establish retained binding or general fragment-linking competitiveness. Anchor-coordinate preservation and broader target coverage are not quantitatively demonstrated.

Generality and reproducibility remain limited. The chemistry covers only 93 building blocks, 19 templates, and short tree-structured assemblies, without scaling experiments. Retrosynthesis estimates use only 100 samples and lack uncertainty intervals. The baseline training description also conflicts: the main text states matched epochs, whereas Appendix C describes 150 epochs and a single conformer per molecule. These issues, together with the sampling inconsistencies and missing decisive baselines, place the current submission below the acceptance threshold despite its promising direction.

strengths: The joint generation of reaction graphs and atomic coordinates addresses a meaningful gap between synthesis-aware molecular design and geometry-conditioned generation. Reaction-center labels and visibility-aware coordinate handling are useful technical contributions.
SYNSPACE is a substantial potential resource: approximately 1.2 million reaction graphs and 7.5 million conformers, with documented construction procedures and two vocabulary sizes.

Unconditional results are promising: 96.7% chemical validity, 87.2% PoseBusters validity, and improved retrosynthesis solve rates. Evaluation includes multiple geometry metrics, two retrosynthesis systems, conditional tasks, and training and sampling ablations.

Pharmacophore conditioning and fragment linking demonstrate useful flexibility without target-specific training. Comparisons with synthesis-aware and geometry-aware baselines address relevant competing approaches.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. The categorical probabilities in Equations 14–15 do not normalize as written and disagree with Equation 2. Section B.12 specifies alpha(t)=exp(-10^8 t), which would keep essentially all discrete variables masked until the final step, conflicting with the reported distinction between ordinary sampling and FinalOnly. Algorithm 4 also omits the time-dependent divisor expected when converting clean-coordinate predictions into the stated linear-interpolation flow. These may be documentation errors, but the implemented process must be clarified before technical soundness and reproducibility can be established.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the benefit of joint modeling. Most unconditional baselines use different training distributions. The principal same-dataset control, SemlaFlow, uses one conformer per molecule, whereas SYNCOGEN samples conformers during training; its training duration is also inconsistently reported. A matched synthesis-graph generator followed by a conformer generator is missing. The FinalOnly sampling ablation does not substitute for this comparison.

Claims of guaranteed or readily executable synthesis exceed the evidence. Appendix A.1 explicitly omits protecting-group requirements, directing effects, and stoichiometric complications; reaction-generated stereoisomers also share the same graph representation. Retrosynthesis solve rates assess whether another system finds a route, rather than whether the generated route is executable. Experimental synthesis is not essential for this contribution, but systematic validation of proposed routes and more qualified claims are needed.

The conformer-quality claims are stronger than the metrics support. The reported xTB quantity is dispersion energy alone, not total conformational energy or strain, so a more negative value does not establish a more realistic conformer. Table 6 shows mixed distributional fidelity, including worse xTB-energy distribution matching than every listed baseline. PoseBusters performance ties the original SemlaFlow rather than surpassing it.

Conditional superiority is not consistently demonstrated. In Table 8, zero-shot fragment-linking validity is only 46.9–57.6%, versus 93.7–95.8% for DiffLinker, and PoseBusters results are mixed. Pharmacophore comparisons use different conditioning inputs and molecule-size protocols across methods, with only 100 samples per target. Docking scores and selected AlphaFold3 examples do not establish high-affinity binding or quantify preservation of the requested pharmacophore geometry.

Statistical and generalization evidence remains limited. Although baseline results average three sampling runs, uncertainty is not reported, including for retrosynthesis estimates based on only 100 molecules. Scaling from 93 to 378 building blocks reduces PoseBusters validity from 82.8% to 65.0%, weakening the claim of scaling with little sacrifice. The substantial engineering contribution is promising, but these evaluation gaps and the unresolved method specification leave the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap: jointly generating molecular geometry and explicit reaction-based representations. The building-block representation, compatibility constraints, and handling of unknown atom counts form a meaningful application-specific contribution.
SYNSPACE is a substantial potential resource, containing approximately 1.2 million molecular graphs and 7.5 million conformers, with documented construction procedures and two vocabulary sizes.

Unconditional generation results are promising: Table 1 reports 96.7% chemical validity, 87.2% PoseBusters validity, and improved retrosynthesis solve rates. The comparison with SemlaFlow trained on SYNSPACE provides useful evidence beyond comparisons across datasets.

The evaluation covers unconditional generation, fragment linking, and pharmacophore conditioning, and includes several training and sampling ablations. Amortized conditional generation without target-specific retraining is practically attractive.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains substantial unresolved inconsistencies. The categorical probabilities in Equations 14–15 sum to 1/(1−α_t), rather than one, and disagree with Equation 2. Section B.12 specifies α_t=exp(−10^8 t), which would leave essentially every discrete variable masked until the final sampling step, contradicting the distinction between the default and FinalOnly experiments. Algorithm 4 also omits the 1/t factor required for the stated linear interpolation when predicting clean coordinates. These may be documentation errors, but they prevent faithful reproduction and undermine confidence in the stated method.

The central synthesizability claims exceed the evidence. Appendix A.1 explicitly omits protection requirements, directing effects, and stoichiometry with multiple reaction centers, while reaction-generated stereoisomers collapse to one graph representation. Template compatibility therefore does not ensure an executable synthesis. Retrosynthesis solve rates support relative accessibility but do not validate the particular routes returned by the model; the claims of guaranteed, streamlined synthesis require qualification and route-level validation.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the benefit of joint generation. Most unconditional baselines use a different training distribution, and the matched SemlaFlow comparison uses a single conformer per molecule, whereas SYNCOGEN samples conformers during training. Training duration is also inconsistently reported across Sections 5.1, B.14, and C.1. A matched reaction-graph generator followed by conventional or learned conformer generation is missing; FinalOnly inference on a jointly trained model is not an adequate substitute.

Several geometry claims overstate the results. Section D.4 defines the xTB metric as dispersion energy alone, which cannot establish overall conformational quality, particularly across different molecular compositions. Table 6 shows that SYNCOGEN is not consistently best at reproducing geometry distributions and has the largest xTB-energy distribution discrepancy among the listed methods. Table 7 also favors RDKit on both reported conformer metrics.

Conditional evaluation remains limited and partly confounded. Fragment linking uses only three selected complexes; Table 8 reports substantially lower validity for zero-shot SYNCOGEN (46.9–57.6%) than DiffLinker (93.7–95.8%), with worse PoseBusters validity on two targets. Pharmacophore evaluation primarily measures docking after redocking, without quantitative pharmacophore satisfaction or preservation of generated poses. Baselines receive different conditioning information and size settings, and docking scores and selected AlphaFold3 overlays do not establish high-affinity binding.

Uncertainty and scalability are insufficiently characterized. Retrosynthesis estimates use only 100 samples without confidence intervals, and reported averages lack variability despite repeated sampling. Scaling the vocabulary from 93 to 378 blocks reduces PoseBusters validity from 82.8% to 65.0% and chemical validity from 93.5% to 87.0%, which weakens the claim of little quality sacrifice. Overall, the promising contribution is outweighed by unresolved specification errors and insufficiently controlled evidence for the strongest claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap: jointly generating molecular geometry and explicit synthesis-oriented representations. Reaction-center-aware building-block graphs and visibility-aware coordinate modeling form a meaningful application-specific contribution.
SYNSPACE is a substantial potential resource, containing approximately 1.2 million molecular graphs and 7.5 million conformers, with two vocabulary sizes and pharmacophore annotations.

Unconditional results are promising: SYNCOGEN reports 96.7% chemical validity, 87.2% PoseBusters validity, and improved retrosynthesis solve rates. Comparison with SemlaFlow retrained on SYNSPACE provides useful evidence beyond comparisons across different datasets.

The evaluation spans unconditional generation, fragment linking, and pharmacophore conditioning, with additional constraint, sampling, and vocabulary ablations. Target-conditioned generation without target-specific retraining is practically appealing.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains substantial unresolved inconsistencies. Equations (14–15) give categorical probability vectors whose entries sum to 1/(1−α_t), rather than one. Section B.12 specifies α_t=exp(−10^8 t), which would leave essentially every discrete variable masked until the endpoint at the reported sampling resolution. Algorithm 4 also omits the 1/t factor required for the stated linear-path, clean-coordinate-prediction flow update. These may be documentation errors, but they prevent reproduction of the claimed algorithm and require reconciliation with the implementation.

The contribution of joint modeling is not adequately isolated. Most baselines use different training distributions, while the same-data SemlaFlow comparison uses one conformer per molecule rather than SYNCOGEN’s randomly sampled conformers. Its training duration is also inconsistently described. A synthesis-constrained graph generator followed by a separate conformer generator is an important missing baseline; the FinalOnly inference ablation does not substitute for a properly trained sequential model.

Claims of ensured synthesizability exceed the evidence. Appendix A.1 explicitly omits protection requirements, directing effects, and competing reaction-center behavior, and simplifies some building blocks. Template compatibility and independent retrosynthesis success do not establish that the generated routes themselves are executable. Representative expert route assessment or experimental validation would strengthen this central claim.

The geometry metrics do not establish uniform state-of-the-art performance. Section D.4 identifies the reported xTB metric as dispersion energy alone, which is not a general measure of conformational quality and remains composition-dependent despite per-atom normalization. Table 6 shows weaker distribution matching than several baselines on multiple metrics. Table 7’s coverage definition measures generated-to-reference proximity rather than reference-ensemble coverage.

Conditional-generation evidence is encouraging but limited. Docking after pose search and selected AlphaFold3 overlays do not directly demonstrate preservation of generated poses, pharmacophore satisfaction, or binding affinity. Comparisons use different conditioning information and size-selection procedures. Fragment linking covers only three selected ligands, and zero-shot chemical validity is 46.9–57.6%, substantially below DiffLinker’s 93.7–95.8%; this tradeoff deserves more prominent treatment.

Uncertainty and scalability remain insufficiently characterized. Retrosynthesis evaluations use only 100 samples, without reported confidence intervals; the stated repeated unconditional runs are not accompanied by variability estimates. Expanding the vocabulary reduces PoseBusters validity from 82.8% to 65.0%, weakening the claim of little quality sacrifice. Overall, the promising concept and results do not yet outweigh the specification and evaluation gaps for acceptance.
